messages.content: Can you retrieve the weather forecast for White Plains for next week with temperatures in Celsius?

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.reasoning:
We need to call the function requests_get with appropriate params. The user wants forecast for White Plains next week with temperatures in Celsius. We need to get coordinates for White Plains. White Plains likely refers to White Plains, New York. Coordinates approx 41.0535°N, -73.7629°W. Use Open-Meteo API. For forecast, we can use "forecast" endpoint. According to Open-Meteo docs, endpoint: https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast. Parameters: latitude, longitude, daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min, etc. Also timezone. For next week, we can set start_date and end_date. But maybe just fetch daily forecast for next 7 days. We'll set daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min. And also specify temperature_unit=celsius. Actually Open-Meteo uses units automatically based on parameter "temperature_unit". Let's check: In Open-Meteo, you can set "temperature_unit=celsius" or "fahrenheit". So we add param temperature_unit=celsius. Also "daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min". Also "timezone=auto" or "America/New_York". We'll set timezone=America/New_York.

Also we might want to set "start_date" and "end_date". But if not set, defaults to today. We can set start_date to tomorrow? Or we can just fetch next 7 days including today. The user said next week. We'll set start_date to tomorrow. But we don't know today's date. We could compute using python datetime. But we can't run code here. We can approximate by setting start_date to 2026-07-09? Wait current date is 2026-07-08. Next week would be 2026-07-09 to 2026-07-15. So we set start_date=2026-07-09, end_date=2026-07-15. That covers next week. We'll set daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min. Also "temperature_unit=celsius".

Thus function call:

{
  url: "https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json", "Accept": "application/json" },
  timeout: 10.0,
  params: {
    latitude: 41.0535,
    longitude: -73.7629,
    daily: "temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min",
    temperature_unit: "celsius",
    timezone: "America/New_York",
    start_date: "2026-07-09",
    end_date: "2026-07-15"
  }
}

We don't need allow_redirects, auth, cert, cookies, proxies, stream, verify. They have defaults.

So we call the function.
